title: Pain
path: First Aid Management of Patients with Medical and Surgical Emergencies

headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Pain
headings.content: Pain is universally defined as an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage. This classic definition, established by the International Association for the Study of Pain, highlights that pain is not merely a physical sensation but a complex multidimensional phenomenon. It possesses sensory, cognitive, and affective components, meaning two individuals with identical physical injuries may perceive and report discomfort quite differently. A foundational clinical axiom in nursing states that pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, and exists whenever they say it does. This subjective nature makes patient self-report the gold standard of assessment, even when objective vital signs remain entirely normal.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Mechanisms of Pain
headings.content:
The journey of pain from a damaged tissue to the conscious brain involves four distinct physiological processes: transduction, transmission, modulation, and perception.

1. **Transduction**: Specialized sensory receptors called **nociceptors** detect thermal, mechanical, or chemical stimuli and convert them into electrical nerve impulses.
2. **Transmission**: These electrical signals travel along peripheral nerve fibers—specifically fast, myelinated **A-delta fibers** for sharp pain and slow, unmyelinated **C fibers** for dull, aching pain—toward the spinal cord and up to the thalamus.
3. **Modulation**: The central nervous system can alter pain signals along the pathway through descending inhibitory neurons that release endogenous opioids like endorphins and enkephalins.
4. **Perception**: The cerebral cortex finally interprets the signals, giving rise to the conscious awareness and emotional reaction of suffering.

headings.title: Classifications and Types of Pain
headings.content:
Pain is categorized by its duration, underlying mechanism, and anatomical location to guide appropriate clinical interventions. Acute pain serves as a biological warning sign, lasting a short duration and resolving as damaged tissue heals. Chronic pain persists beyond normal healing time, typically defined as lasting longer than three to six months, and often serves no protective biological purpose. Mechanistically, pain splits into nociceptive and neuropathic categories.

- **Nociceptive Pain**: Arises from actual or threatened damage to non-neural tissue and is further divided into somatic (localized to skin, bones, or muscles) and visceral (arising from internal organs, often cramping or poorly localized).
- **Neuropathic Pain**: Caused by a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory nervous system itself, characterized by burning, shooting, or electric-shock sensations.

headings.title: Comprehensive Pain Assessment and Measurement
headings.content:
Evaluating pain requires a systematic approach using validated tools suited to the patient's developmental stage, cognitive status, and cultural background. The standard mnemonic **PQRSTU** provides a thorough clinical framework for subjective history taking: Provocative/palliative factors, Quality, Region/radiation, Severity, Timing, and Understanding/impact on the patient.

| Tool Name | Target Patient Population | Key Feature |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Numeric Rating Scale (NRS)** | Adults with intact cognition | Rates pain from 0 to 10 |
| **Faces Pain Scale - Revised** | Children or language barriers | Uses facial expressions |
| **FLACC Behavioral Scale** | Infants and non-verbal adults | Observes Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability |

Forgetting to reassess pain after intervention is a common clinical pitfall in busy Nigerian hospital wards; documentation must capture both baseline and post-intervention scores.

headings.title: Pharmacological Management of Pain
headings.content:
Pharmacotherapy for pain follows the World Health Organization analgesic ladder, moving step-by-step from non-opioids to strong opioids depending on pain severity. Mild pain is managed with non-opioid analgesics such as paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or diclofenac. When pain persists or increases, weak opioids such as tramadol or codeine are introduced. Severe pain requires potent opioids like morphine or fentanyl.

Adjuvant medications, originally developed for other conditions, enhance pain relief for specific etiologies—for instance, gabapentin for neuropathic pain or amitriptyline for chronic muscle tension. Administering analgesics around-the-clock during acute phases prevents pain levels from fluctuating wildly, proving far more effective than waiting for pain to return before administering the next dose.

headings.title: Non-Pharmacological Pain Interventions
headings.content:
Non-pharmacological strategies complement drug therapy by reducing anxiety, muscle tension, and the cortical perception of pain signals. Physical modalities include superficial heat to increase local blood flow and relax spasmed muscles, or cold therapy (cryotherapy) to reduce acute inflammation and numb local nerve endings. Cutaneous stimulation techniques like transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) activate non-painful sensory fibers, closing the spinal gate to pain transmission as explained by the Gate Control Theory.

Cognitive-behavioral approaches such as guided imagery, controlled breathing exercises, distraction, and progressive muscle relaxation empower patients by engaging higher brain centers to modulate descending pain pathways.

headings.title: Nursing Responsibilities and Complications in Pain Management
headings.content: Managing pain safely requires vigilant nursing surveillance, particularly when administering potent analgesics. Monitoring for respiratory depression is the primary safety priority when patients receive opioid medications, requiring regular assessment of respiratory rate and depth. Gastrointestinal complications, such as opioid-induced constipation, require prophylactic prescribing of laxatives because tolerance does not develop to this specific side effect. Nurses must also actively address common misconceptions regarding addiction; physical dependence and tolerance are normal physiological adaptations to long-term opioid therapy, distinct from psychological addiction or substance use disorder. Clear patient education regarding side effect management and proper dosage schedules ensures treatment adherence upon discharge.
